content: In mathematics, the domain of a function refers to the set of all possible input values for which the function is defined. When a function is represented in a Cartesian coordinate system, the domain corresponds to the values along the x-axis, also known as the abscissa. For a function ( f: X to Y ), the set ( X ) represents the domain of ( f ), while the set ( Y ) is referred to as the codomain. The range of ( f ) is the set of all actual output values produced by the function, denoted as ( { f(x) : x in X } ). The range may either be identical to the codomain or a proper subset of it. Typically, the range is smaller than the codomain unless the function is surjective (onto). A well-defined function must map every element in its domain to an element in its codomain. For example, consider a function ( f ) that is undefined at ( x = 0 ). In this case, the set of real numbers ( mathbb{R} ) cannot serve as the domain of ( f ). Instead, the domain might be ( mathbb{R} setminus { 0 } ), or the function can be explicitly extended by defining ( f(0) ) to fill the gap. If the definition of ( f ) is extended to include ( x = 0 ), then ( f ) becomes defined for all real numbers, and its domain becomes ( mathbb{R} ). Functions can also be restricted to subsets of their domain. For instance, the restriction of a function ( g: A to B ) to a subset ( S subseteq A ) is denoted as ( g|_S: S to B ). In the context of partial functions, the term domain can have two distinct meanings. Most mathematicians, including those in recursion theory, define the domain of a partial function as the set of all input values ( x ) for which ( f(x) ) is defined. However, some mathematicians, particularly those in category theory, consider the domain of a partial function ( f: X to Y ) to be the entire set ( X ), regardless of whether ( f(x) ) is defined for every ( x ) in ( X ). In category theory, the focus shifts from functions to morphisms, which are abstract arrows between objects. The domain of a morphism is the object from which the arrow originates. In this framework, many set-theoretic concepts related to domains must be reformulated in a more abstract manner. For example, the idea of restricting a morphism to a subset of its domain requires modification. The concept of subobjects is relevant in this context. In real and complex analysis, the term domain refers to an open, connected subset of a real or complex vector space.
